replacements.text: Strongest feature: Craig completes a conditional syllogism: objective moral values exist, illustrated by rape, cruelty, child abuse, love, equality, and self-sacrifice, and their asserted dependence on God entails divine existence. Principal limitation: These examples distinguish morality from acceptability, but demonstrate neither mind-independent objectivity nor the indispensable premise that atheism cannot accommodate objective value, so the inference inherits that controversy. Live burden: Craig must defend uniquely divine grounding against secular realism and command-independence objections, while Flew must articulate a naturalistic foundation preserving normativity rather than merely citing shared standards. Locked score: The exact 79 reflects logical coherence 79, evidence warrant 64, responsiveness 89, relevance and burden 86, precision and clarity 88, and calibration and charity 68, rewarding transparent structure while retaining substantial grounding and warrant deficits.

Strongest feature: Flew exposes tension among omnipotence, desired obedience, freedom, and punishment by asking why power could not constitute persons who choose obedience without coercion. Principal limitation: The proposal assumes, without a freedom theory, that guaranteed right choice remains libertarianly free; ensuring obedience may eliminate alternatives, while the tyrant comparison caricatures divine rationale. Live burden: Flew must specify a mechanism for certain yet free obedience, while Craig must explain why omnipotence and foreknowledge cannot actualize free right choices and why punishment remains compatible with divine perfection. Locked score: The exact 68 reflects logical coherence 65, evidence warrant 56, responsiveness 82, relevance and burden 76, precision and clarity 70, and calibration and charity 53, crediting relevance but discounting unsupported modality, compressed distinctions, and inflammatory framing.
